newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Metals - Singapore zinc premiums dive on stocks.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals - Singapore zinc premiums dive on stocks.

text.p: Singapore zinc premiums have fallen sharply due to a dip in physical demand on soaring London Metal Exchange (LME) prices and on ample stocks of the metal in the city-state, dealers said on Wednesday.
"LME prices are high but on the physical side there are no takers", Vinod Kumar, director of Singapore-based metal company Donald Mcarthy, told Reuters. "This is basically fund buying."
Dealers quoted Singapore zinc premiums at between $3-$5 a tonne over LME cash prices compared with $10-$15 last week.
Three-month zinc was at a new 6-3/4 year high in early LME trade on Wednesday and was testing resistance at $1,450.
Kumar estimated the volume of zinc stocks in Singapore, off LME warrant, at around 25,000 tonnes, while another dealer put the figure at between 15,000-20,000 tonnes.
"The premium in Singapore is low because the metal is freely available in the region," the dealer said.
"There is plenty of metal on warrant in Singapore. In Europe and the U.S. it has firmed up purely because people are looking to source metal at LME," he added.
LME zinc stocks fell a further 1,475 tonnes on Wednesday after a 950-tonne drop on Tuesday to total 423,100 tonnes, which included a fall in exchange inventories in Singapore to 31,525.
"Personally, I think the fund managers are playing a big part in the stock reduction," another dealer said. "I am very very surprised at what is going on."

U.S. dealers said on Tuesday that there is a tussle in the zinc market between a major trade house, said to be holding a large long position in physical metal, and Chinese operators who are short and saddled with some metal which is no longer LME-deliverable and which may have to be re-refined.
They added that one Chinese smelter has also sold forward some 60,000 tonnes of extra metal for export all at once.
"Before they actually have to deliver, they are going to have to roll it over into the first few months of the year, which is happening now," one U.S. broker said.
On Monday China's Zhuzhou smelter said Swiss trader Glencore had withdrawn a complaint made to the LME about the quality of its Torch brand of zinc.
Zhuzhou said the quality claim would not affect its zinc shipments, which totalled 16,000 tonnes in June, to the physical market and the LME warehouse in Singapore.
"The key (for future price moves) is how much Chinese material we see in the market," one Japanese dealer said.
"We also heard china is covering parts of its shorts. they are delivering zinc to cover their lost positions."
The dealer added that zinc producers were very bullish and were talking about three-month LME zinc reaching $1,800.

"Here in Japan, you feel the market is tight...we hear exports of galvanized steel to China are doing quite well, helped by the yen's fall (against the dollar). A fall in domestic car sales is also offset by exports," he said.
Dealers said no major changes in Singapore aluminium premiums were expected.
"It (aluminium) is very well steady but nothing spectacular," one dealer said.
He said Singapore was a liquid market, but since not much material was flowing into the city, premiums should remain at similar levels for some time.
Dealers said premiums for Western 20-25 kg ingots were quoted at between US$80-$85 a tonne over LME cash prices agaisnt a quote of $85-90 a week ago.
Indian and Russian aluminium ingots were fetched premiums of between $60-$65 after hovering at $55-65 recently, they said.
